blocks.text: — — — — τοί δ' ἐκέχυντο Ἀκρίσι καρποβόροις ἐναλίγκιοι, αἵ τε φέρονται Ὡς νέφος, ἢ πολὺς ὄμβρος ὑπὲρ χθονὸς εὐρυπέδοιο, Ἄπλητοι, μερόπεσσιν ἀεικέα λοιμὸν ἄγουσαι· [— — — — toi d' ekechynto Akrisi karpoborois enalinkioi, hai te pherontai Hōs nephos, ē polys ombros hyper chthonos eurypedoio, Aplētoi, meropessin aeikea loimon agousai]

But they poured themselves forth, like crop-devouring locusts, which are borne along like a cloud, or a heavy rain over the broad earth, countless, bringing a dreadful famine upon men. For otherwise, when men are compared to locusts, this serves to express contempt, and πρὸς τὸν ἐξουθενισμόν [pros ton exouthenismon]. Such is the statement about the Israelites when compared with the Anakim giants, Num. XIII, 34. Compared with them we seemed like locusts. And about men in comparison with God, Es. XL, 22. He who sits upon the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts. Not unlike this is Lucian's phrase in the Hermotimus, Οἷον μύρμηκας ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕψους ἐπισκοποῦντάς τινας τοὺς ἄλλους [Hoion myrmēkas apo tou hypsous episkopountas tinas tous allous], Looking down from on high upon other men as if upon ants. Thus you will nowhere see great empires compared with these little animals, but rather with lions, leopards and bears, as in the seventh chapter of Daniel. But to make the matter clearer, let us now examine what follows.
In verse 5, Awake, you drunkards (for whom long drinking usually brings on sleep, [III, 293] — — and from the wine sense returns to their breasts,

as we read in the Poet); weep and wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth] As below in verse 9, The sacrifice is cut off. And in verse 16, Before our eyes the food is cut off. Namely by the locusts, one species of which is called גזם gazam from cutting off. But the Prophet here uses the verb כרת, as in Nahum III, 15. תכריתך, the sword shall cut you off, and shall consume you like the bruchus.

In verse 6, For a nation has come up against my land, strong and without number. Its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of a lioness.] On which Abarbanel says, לא אמר הנביא זה באמת על הארבה כי איך יקראהו גוי וקהל גוים, The Prophet certainly did not say this of the locusts: for how could he call them a nation, and an assembly of nations? But the Prophet had someone to follow, the wisest of kings, whose words are Prov. XXX, 25. 26. הנמלים עם לא עז, The ants, a people not strong. And, שפנים עם לא עצום, The choerogrylli, a people not mighty. For what he cites there from the Midrash is ridiculous, namely that in that passage too Solomon signified four empires by the four little animals. I admit, indeed, that the word nation is properly used of man, and is not transferred to beasts except by metaphor. But nothing is more common than that metaphor. Hence the most ancient of poets, and also the best, said in Iliad β´, verse 87,
Ἠΰτε ἔθνεα εἶσι μελισσάων ἁδινάων, [Ēute ethnea eisi melissaōn hadinaōn]
As go the nations of thronging bees. Where the Scholiast says, Πρώτη δὲ αὕτη παραβολὴ τῷ ποιητῇ· [Prōtē de hautē parabolē tō poiētē]. And verse 458,
— — ὀρνίθων πετεηνῶν ἔθνεα πολλὰ, Χηνῶν, ἢ γεράνων, ἢ κύκνων δουλιχοδείρων. [— — ornithōn peteēnōn ethnea polla, Chēnōn, ē geranōn, ē kyknōn doulichodeirōn]
Many nations of winged birds, of geese, or cranes, or long-necked swans. [col. 468] And verse 469,
Ἠΰτε μυιάων ἁδινάων ἔθνεα πολλὰ, [Ēute myiaōn hadinaōn ethnea polla]
As the many nations of thronging flies. And Odyssey ξ, verse 73, of the pigsties,
— — — ἔνθ᾽ ἔθνεα ἔρχατο χοίρων, [— — — enth' ethnea erchato choirōn]
Where the nations of swine were penned. And Orpheus, On Stones, in the section on Coral,
Ἔκ τε μύων ἀγέλας, ἐκ τ᾽ ἀκρίδος ἄπλετον ἔθνος Ῥαίσει. — — — — — [Ek te myōn agelas, ek t' akridos apleton ethnos Rhaisei. — — — — —]

And it will destroy the herds of mice, and the boundless nation of locusts. Oppian also, near the beginning of book 3 of the Cynegetica, [III, 294] Ἀλλ᾽ ὅτε δὴ κεραῶν ἠείσαμεν ἔθνεα θήρων, [All' hote dē keraōn ēeisamen ethnea thērōn]
But after we have sung the nations of horned beasts. And Lucillius, book 2 of the Anthology, chapter 26,
Ὄψει καὶ γυπῶν ἔθνεα, καὶ κοράκων· [Opsei kai gypōn ethnea, kai korakōn]
You will see nations of both vultures and ravens. And Pisides in the Hexaemeron,
Τίς ἐκστρατεύει παγγενῆ τὴν ἀκρίδα, Ἔθνος πτερωτὸν, εἰς φθορὰν Αἰγυπτίων; [Tis ekstrateuei pangenē tēn akrida, Ethnos pterōton, eis phthoran Aigyptiōn?]
Who marshals the locust of every kind, a winged nation, for the destruction of the Egyptians? Nor do the Latin writers speak otherwise. As when the Poet says of horses in book 3 of the Georgics,
Only those whom you shall choose to rear for the hope of the race [gentis].
And of calves,
— — they brand on them marks and the names of the race [gentis].
Such too is the passage in the same place where the plague seizes
The hope and the flock together, and the whole race [gentem] from its origin:
that is, the whole fold. As when in book 4 the fish of Proteus are called
— — the watery nation [gens] of the vast sea.
And of bees the same poet in the same place,
— — — and of the whole nation [gentis] in order I shall tell the customs, and pursuits, and peoples, and battles.
And again,
As the kings have two aspects, so do the bodies of the nation [gentis].
And in book 1 of the Aeneid,
— — when they lead forth the full-grown young of the nation [gentis].
